title: Force-with-lease, pull requests and forks
summary: Rewriting a pushed branch needs a force push; --force-with-lease makes it safe. Then the review flow that most teams run on.

steps.title: When you need to force
body: You pushed `feature/coupons`, then rebased it onto the latest `main` (or squashed it). Your new commits are not descendants of the old ones, so a plain push is rejected. You must **force**:
```text
git push --force              # "make the server's branch point at my commit, whatever is there"
git push --force-with-lease   # "...but only if it still points where I last saw it"
The danger with `--force`: if a teammate pushed a commit to that branch since your last fetch, it is silently **thrown away**.
`--force-with-lease` checks the server's tip against your `origin/feature/coupons`. If someone else pushed, it refuses with *stale info*, and you fetch and look before deciding.
> **Tip:** Make `--force-with-lease` your only force. Some people alias it: `git config --global alias.pushf "push --force-with-lease"`.

steps.prompt: You rebased your feature branch and run `git push --force-with-lease`. It is rejected with *stale info*. What happened?
options: Someone pushed to that branch on the server after your last fetch, so your lease (the tip you expected) no longer matches
The server does not allow force pushes
steps.explain: Good news: nothing was lost. Fetch, see what they pushed (`git log feature..origin/feature`), bring it into your branch, and push again.

items: My own feature branch, after a rebase, before review
My PR branch, after squashing in response to review, telling the reviewer
steps.explain: Force-push only branches you own. Protect `main` and release branches on the server so nobody can force-push them, even by accident.

steps.title: Force versus lease
prompt: Model the two force pushes. `serverTip` is where the branch is now on the server; `lastFetched` is your `origin/<branch>`, where you last saw it.
Write `ForcePush(string mode, string newTip, string serverTip, string lastFetched)`:
- `--force-with-lease`: the same if `serverTip == lastFetched`, otherwise `"rejected (stale info)"`.
starter: static string ForcePush(string mode, string newTip, string serverTip, string lastFetched)
solution: static string ForcePush(string mode, string newTip, string serverTip, string lastFetched)
hints: The only difference between the modes is one comparison.
template: Dojo.Eq("teammate pushed since my fetch", "rejected (stale info)", ForcePush("--force-with-lease", "def", "zzz", "abc"));
Dojo.Eq("--force does not care (and destroys zzz)", "forced: zzz -> def", ForcePush("--force", "def", "zzz", "abc"));

steps.title: The pull request flow
body: On GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps, work reaches `main` through a **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request):
```text
1. git switch -c feature/coupons          branch from an up-to-date main
2. commit in small, clear steps
3. git push -u origin feature/coupons
4. open a PR: what, why, how to test, screenshots
5. CI runs build + tests on the PR; reviewers comment
6. push more commits (or rebase + force-with-lease) to address feedback
7. approved + green -> merge (merge commit, squash, or rebase-merge)
8. delete the branch
**Good PRs are small.** A 200-line PR gets a real review; a 2000-line PR gets *"LGTM"*. Split big work into a stack of PRs, or hide it behind a feature flag.
As a reviewer: check behaviour and design first, style last; ask questions instead of issuing orders; approve when it is better than before, not when it is perfect.

steps.prompt: Arrange the steps of a typical pull request.
lines: Commit the fix with a test
Open a pull request describing what and why
Address review comments and wait for CI
steps.explain: Branch, commit, publish, ask for review, iterate, merge.

steps.title: Forks
body: For open source (or anything you cannot push to) you **fork**: the platform copies the repo into your account.
```text
upstream  github.com/dotnet/runtime          the original; you cannot push
|  fork
origin    github.com/you/runtime             your copy; you push here
|  clone
local     your laptop
```text
git clone git@github.com:you/runtime.git
git remote add upstream https://github.com/dotnet/runtime.git
git fetch upstream
git switch -c fix-typo upstream/main      # branch from the real latest
git push -u origin fix-typo               # then open a PR from you:fix-typo to dotnet:main
Keep your fork's `main` current with `git fetch upstream` + `git rebase upstream/main` (or the platform's *Sync fork* button).
